title: Detection of Purchase Technical Data
summary: This detection strategy covers the purchase of technical data, where an adversary buys information such as credentials, network details, source code or telemetry that shortens the work needed for an intrusion. It matters because the purchase itself does not touch your environment, so the only chances to catch it are leak monitoring feeds, credential exposure alerts and behavioural indicators on internal systems such as token use from unexpected locations. The telemetry that makes it possible includes credential exposure and leak monitoring feed entries, identity provider alerts for passwords found in breaches, procurement and finance records for unusual data purchases, and cloud or application audit logs showing credential use without a corresponding login. It fails in practice because mentions in criminal markets are noisy and often stale, so a rule that alerts on any mention produces more work than value unless it is scoped to your live domains and to accounts that still exist.

beginner.definition: The purchase of technical data means an attacker buys information instead of stealing it. They may buy passwords, network diagrams or access to a system. This detection looks for the signs that your data is being sold or used after a sale.
beginner.whyItMatters: Buying data removes the noisy steps that defenders rely on. There is no scan and no failed login to see. The information may be months old, yet still valid. Watching exposure channels and watching how your own credentials are used gives you a way to see it. It also tells you which leaked data is still dangerous.
howItWorks: You subscribe to leak and credential exposure feeds and to breach notification services for your domains.
Those sources are matched against your live account list, so only accounts that still exist create a finding.
On the internal side, the platform watches for credential use that has no matching sign in, such as an application token used from a new address.
Finance and procurement records are checked for data broker purchases that the security team did not approve.
A finding is then triaged by asking one question first: is this account still active and privileged?
beginner.example: Think of a shop that checks its till receipts against the stock list. A receipt for a sold item is normal. A receipt for an item that the shop never had in stock is a sign that someone else is selling from the same warehouse.
takeaways: Purchased data leaves no trace in your network, so exposure feeds are your main early warning.
Match every feed entry against live accounts, because old and disabled accounts create needless noise.
Any confirmed exposure of an active credential should lead to a reset, not only to a ticket.

objectives: Explain why buying technical data reduces the noise an attacker would otherwise create
Identify the feed, finance and identity telemetry that can reveal a data purchase or its use
Match exposure findings against live accounts and assess which are exploitable
Recognise credential use that has no corresponding interactive sign in
Run a credential reset and monitoring plan after a confirmed exposure
dataSources: Credential exposure and leak monitoring feed entries referencing your email domains or account names
Identity provider reports of passwords or secrets found in third party breach data
Application and cloud audit logs showing a token or API key used without a matching interactive sign in
Procurement and expense records for threat intelligence, data broker or credential monitoring purchases
logic: The pattern is a mention of your live accounts, hosts or code in an exposure feed that is followed by evidence of use, such as a valid credential being exercised from an address that never performed an interactive sign in, or an API token used from a new autonomous system number. The fields to correlate are the account or asset named in the feed, whether the account still exists and its privilege level, the source address of the use and the timestamp. The benign case is an old disabled account or a public marketing address appearing in a years old breach dump, while the malicious case shows an active privileged account, a recent dump date and credential use in the days after the mention.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Live credential exposed in leak feed then used from new address
# logsource:
#   product: azure
#   service: signin
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event_type: signin
#     user_principal_name|in: exposed_accounts_live
#     result_type: 0
#   filter:
#     source_ip|in: known_office_ranges
#     device_compliant: true
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: high
falsePositives: A public relations or recruitment mailbox that appears in marketing lists and scraped data without any compromise
A password manager audit that flags a reused credential the user has already started changing
A security research purchase of aggregated breach data by the internal threat intelligence team
A shared application token that legitimately calls the API from a new cloud region after a migration
tuningNotes: Filter feed entries to email domains and asset names you actually own, and require that the account is enabled and privileged before alerting. Baseline the addresses each application token normally uses so first use stands out. You lose early warning for data sold about systems you do not track, so maintain the asset list from the configuration management database and review unmatched feed entries monthly rather than in real time.
